title: Regulated Deployments: Field Ops Messaging & Competitive Map
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact field-reference for AEs and SEs engaging regulated buyers (finance, healthcare, gov). Focus: clear, plain-language messaging about VPC/on-prem control plane choices, how we minimize audit surface and telemetry, and short, battle-tested responses to the most frequent concerns.

Audience:
- Account Execs running discovery calls
- Solutions Engineers scoping PoCs and architecture
- GTM managers who need consistent language for pricing and contract asks

Elevator positioning (single-line):
Redwood Private gives you the same inference API and operational tooling as our hosted product, but with a customer-controlled control plane and data flow that aligns with regulated security policies — so you get predictable performance without widening your compliance footprint.

How to describe the control-plane choices (short, direct):
- Hosted control plane (standard): Redwood manages the control plane and telemetry, minimal ops for the customer, good for low-risk apps and speed to production.
- Customer-managed control plane (VPC/private): Control-plane endpoints are deployed in the customer's cloud or on-prem environment. Metadata, service discovery, and orchestration control are kept inside the customer's network; Redwood support operates over an authenticated management channel only when customers permit.
- Air-gapped/on-prem package: Full control plane and data plane remain inside customer networks; upgrades, observability export, and support interactions occur via pre-approved packages and offline handoffs.

Plain-language assurances buyers expect (and how we phrase them):
- No exfiltration: "By default we do not send model inputs or outputs to Redwood cloud — logs and metrics can be retained locally or forwarded to your SIEM on your terms."
- Key custody: "We integrate with your KMS/HSM; you control keys and rotation policies; Redwood never stores unencrypted model keys."
- Audit trail: "We provide local audit logging with tamper-evident mechanisms and standard export formats for SCCF/CSV ingestion into your auditing tools."
- Minimal telemetry: "Default telemetry is limited to health and capacity; samples for quality monitoring are opt-in and anonymized."

Common buyer concerns and concise rebuttals (fast scripts):
1) Concern: "How do we know you won't collect data later?"
   Quick reply: "Control-plane artifacts and logs are under your tenancy. Any telemetry flow to Redwood is explicit and requires config and an opt-in agreement; we can show the exact fields and a data-flow diagram during the PoC."

2) Concern: "We need to demonstrate segmentation and no outbound internet."
   Quick reply: "Our air-gapped install contains both control and data planes inside your VPC/on-prem. Support interactions occur through presigned bundles or via a customer-controlled bastion."

3) Concern: "What about model updates and security patches?"
   Quick reply: "We provide signed update bundles and an upgrade checklist. Customers can run upgrades on their cadence; we also offer an optional managed upgrade service that runs in your tenancy under an agreed maintenance window."

4) Concern: "How is SLA handled if everything is on-prem?"
   Quick reply: "For Dedicated and Private deployments we offer contractual SLAs tied to configuration and validated operational runbooks. The SLA scope and on-call matrix are defined in the contract and verified during handover."

Competitive map (short):
- CloudAIInc: Sells hosted endpoints; weak story for private control planes — good for quick pilots, poor for regulated buyers.
- EdgeServe: Focused on on-prem inference runtime but lacks a unified API and rollout tooling; puts more ops burden on customers.
- OpenRuntime (open-source stacks): Flexible but requires heavy internal engineering to reach production economics; limited vendor support for compliance audits.
- Redwood positioning compared: Unified API + optional customer-managed control plane + signed offline bundles + clear audit exports. Emphasize lower ops overhead vs pure OSS and stronger compliance posture vs hosted-only competitors.

Field playbook: PoC checklist (what SEs should request early)
- Extract: compliance contact, network security owner, identity owner, KMS owner, app owner, and legal.
- Ask for: sample network diagram, allowed outbound ports, SIEM ingestion method, existing key providers, and retention rules.
- Minimum PoC topology: 1 control-plane node in customer VPC or air-gap; 1 data-plane GPU node (can be in same VPC); a temporary monitoring sink (customer-hosted) for audit logs.
- Deliverables within 3 weeks: deployment manifest, signed upgrade bundle, test prompts for quality validation, operational runbook with rollback steps.

Pricing/contract language to reduce friction (AE scripts):
- "We price Private as a platform fee + a predictably sized compute commitment; you only pay for the capacity you reserve. We can start with a 90-day pilot with a capped monthly minimum to validate throughput and observability."
- For legal: "We can include specific audit and data-handling clauses; we have standard addenda for KMS, data residency, and code escrow."

Escalation and support model (how to explain to buyers):
- Default: Redwood provides a named SE and an implementation engineer for the onboarding window.
- Optional: 24x7 managed ops with runbook takeover per contract.
- Incident model: Customer-owned triage; Redwood provides runbook-backed guidance and signed hotfixes.

Quick objection scripts (short bullets for reps to memorize):
- "We can't allow external telemetry": "Understood — we will disable telemetry by default; any exports require your explicit authorization."
- "We need to keep keys in our HSM": "Supported. We integrate with your HSM and never store unwrapped keys."
- "What if you go down?": "We support multi-region bursting and can failover to a cached variant or a lower-cost local model variant depending on your SLOs."

Example email template (post-demo, succinct):
Subject: Follow-up & PoC next steps — Redwood Private
Body: Thanks for your time today. As discussed, next steps are: 1) share network diagram & KMS owner contact, 2) agree pilot scope (3 weeks), and 3) confirm allowed maintenance windows. I've attached our short PoC checklist and a sample signed update manifest for review.

Appendix: quick technical notes for SEs (bulleted)
- Telemetry fields we may need to collect for operational excellence: instance_id, request_latency, error_rate — all can be toggled off or sent to your SIEM only.
- Audit export formats: JSON LTS, CSV, Syslog via TCP TLS.
- KMS integrations: AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, Vault HSM via PKCS#11.
- Upgrade mechanism: signed tarball + SHA256 validation + optional ephemeral agent that performs checksum and upgrade under a controlled window.

What to do next (team actions):
- SEs: use this doc as the canonical quick-reference for regulated buyer calls; log gaps and new objections to RD-1423.
- Product: iterate on the opt-in telemetry UI so customers can see precise fields before enabling.
- Legal: prepare a short addendum template for air-gapped installs that lists responsibilities and signed delivery artifacts.

Notes and open questions (for future drafts):
- How granular should our default telemetry be for proactive incident detection vs customer comfort?
- Consider shipping a minimal encrypted attestation file customers can review to validate binary provenance at install time.

"Field ops" shorthand: keep answers short, own the operational plan, and offer concrete artifacts (signed bundles, runbooks, export samples). This doc should help close regulated accounts faster by removing vagueness and replacing it with concrete, customer-controlled options.
